opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to where the real bottleneck is right now. If you look at the robotics stack, the hardware side, the joints, the motors, the bodies, has been moving very fast, and there's a strong manufacturing ecosystem behind it. But when you put a capable body in a real home or a real factory, it still doesn't know what to do. It can't generalize. It can do one demo beautifully and then fail when the lighting changes or the object is slightly different. So the gap isn't really the body anymore; it's the brain.

For us, coming from a background in vision and generative models, that's also where we feel we can contribute the most. A lot of what a robot brain needs is understanding the 3D world, predicting how things will change, imagining the consequences of an action before taking it. These are things we've spent years working on in perception and world modeling, so it's a natural extension rather than starting from zero.

There's also a strategic reason. The brain layer is the part that can be shared across many different bodies. If you build a good foundation model for embodied intelligence, it can serve a humanoid, a robot arm, a mobile platform, and the value compounds as more data flows back. Whereas if you lock yourself into one hardware form, you're betting on that form winning. We'd rather be the layer that makes all of them smarter.

And honestly, I think it's the hardest and most interesting problem. Language models showed that if you get the data and the scaling right, generalization emerges. Nobody has fully cracked that for the physical world yet. The data is scarce, it's expensive, and the feedback loop is slow. That's exactly why it's worth focusing on: whoever figures out how to get general-purpose intelligence into the physical world, that's going to define the next era of robotics.

r002.rationale: It describes a foundation model serving humanoids, robot arms, and mobile platforms, but does not say Lingbo aims to supply the brain for household robots across different hardware brands.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest starting point is that the robot industry today has plenty of bodies and not enough brains. If you look at the hardware side, the supply chain has matured fast. Motors, reducers, sensors, dexterous hands, bipedal and wheeled platforms, you can source almost all of it, and the cost curve is coming down every quarter. So the bottleneck is no longer "can we build a machine that moves." The bottleneck is "can that machine understand what it is seeing, decide what to do, and actually generalize to a situation it has not been scripted for."

That is a software problem, and more specifically it is a model problem. And it happens to be the problem my background prepared me for. I spent years in generative modeling and visual foundation models, learning how to get a network to build a usable internal representation of the world from raw pixels. A robot brain is really that same question pushed one step further: perception, plus understanding of physical and spatial structure, plus turning that understanding into action. So when we started Lingbo, it felt natural to focus on the layer where we had a real edge rather than compete on mechanical engineering where many excellent teams already exist.

There is also a strategic reason. If you tie the brain to one body, you inherit that body's limits. Every hardware form factor today is still a bet, and nobody knows which ones will win. A brain layer that can sit on top of different embodiments lets us learn from all of them, which matters because data is the scarcest resource in this field. The more diverse the bodies and scenarios feeding back into the model, the faster the model improves. That flywheel is very hard to spin if you are a vertically integrated company shipping a single product.

And finally, I think this is where the value will concentrate over time. In computing, the chips and the enclosures became commodities, and the operating system and the intelligence captured the margin. I expect embodied AI to follow a similar path. The companies that own the general-purpose capability to perceive, reason, and act will define what the hardware is for, not the other way around. So we chose to be the brain because that is where the hardest unsolved problem is, where our team is strongest, and where we believe the leverage sits.

r001.rationale: The response links a general-purpose brain layer to uncertainty about which robot form factors will win, but it does not specify household robots.

r002.rationale: The response says the brain layer can work across different embodiments, but it does not state an ambition to supply brains for household robots across hardware brands.

astra-6.text:
Because the brain is what connects a robot’s physical capabilities to useful work. A robot can have excellent motors and sensors, but it still needs to understand what’s happening, decide what to do, and adjust when something doesn’t go as expected.

That’s why I see this as the right focus for Lingbo. If every task requires a carefully scripted sequence, deployment becomes very difficult. The opportunity is to build intelligence that can learn across tasks and environments, so we don’t have to start from scratch each time.

Of course, you can’t develop that intelligence in isolation from the hardware. You need real robots, real tasks, and feedback from failures. But the brain is where we see the opportunity to turn those experiences into capabilities that can be reused.

r001.rationale: It describes adapting to unexpected situations and learning across environments, but does not connect the robot-brain focus to uncertainty about the eventual physical form of household robots.

sol-6.1.text:
I see the robot brain as the layer that connects what a robot can physically do with what people actually need it to do. A capable body is essential, but the robot still has to understand a task, perceive its surroundings, decide what to do, and adapt when something changes.

For Lingbo, that makes the brain a compelling focus. If we can build capabilities that transfer across tasks and different robot bodies, we can reduce the amount of engineering needed for each new application. The challenge is making that transfer work reliably in the physical world. That’s where I think the core value lies.
